section_summary: This section records the United States decision to authorize a second SCAP-controlled, Japanese-manned Antarctic whaling expedition for 1947–48 and protests from Britain, Australia, Norway and New Zealand. It includes proposed alternatives, diplomatic replies, the authorization directive, a press release, and reports of debate in the Far Eastern Commission. Other documents address Japanese fishing areas, crabmeat imports, possible American investment in fisheries, and 1946 whaling statistics.

subfiles.title: Preliminary consultation on Japanese Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Allied representatives objected to another Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition during a preliminary consultation with Hilldring.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages record British, Australian, Norwegian and New Zealand objections concerning catch limits, oil yield, security and economic effects. Hilldring said he would consult the representatives again before final action.

subfiles.title: Arguments for authorizing a second Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: Proposes replies to British objections and flags a possible conflict over a third factory ship.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that Japanese whaling should proceed under SCAP supervision and international rules. It warns that using three vessels could appear inconsistent with a December 1946 assurance about stopping conversion of a tanker.

subfiles.title: Norwegian figures on Japanese whale oil yield
subfiles.about: Lykke compares Japanese and Norwegian whale oil yields and predicts a loss to world supply.
subfiles.summary: Norwegian expeditions reportedly produced 116.5 barrels per blue whale unit against 78.5 on SCAP expeditions. Lykke estimates that another Japanese catch of 1,200 units could reduce world whale oil output by about 7,600 tons.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lykke on whale oil yield
subfiles.about: Hilldring disputes the implication that another Japanese expedition would yield markedly less oil.
subfiles.summary: Citing information from Tokyo, Hilldring says corrected figures and equipment improvements should make Japanese yields compare favorably with those of other countries.

subfiles.title: Rumor concerning crabmeat imports from Japan
subfiles.about: Officials discuss and discount a rumor that 400,000 cases of Japanese crabmeat will be imported.
subfiles.summary: USCC expected at most nine or ten thousand cases; Tyson planned to counter the industry rumor.

subfiles.title: Request to delay public action on whaling authorization
subfiles.about: Requests no public action on the expedition until June 17 while protests are considered.
subfiles.summary: Draft War Department message asks SCAP to delay public action without withdrawing authorization.

subfiles.title: American fishing interests in Japan
subfiles.about: National Canners Association explores investment and contracting possibilities in Japanese fisheries.
subfiles.summary: Whitman advises caution pending reparations decisions and suggests supplying a market and working capital for Japanese products. He notes political sensitivity around salmon and crab fishing.

subfiles.title: SCAP asks where whaling announcement should be made
subfiles.about: SCAP awaits permission to proceed and asks whether Washington or Tokyo should announce authorization.
subfiles.summary: No executive action had yet been taken in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: British protest against second Japanese expedition
subfiles.about: Britain protests authorization and asks that it be withheld or cancelled.
subfiles.summary: The note says the decision conflicts with consultation assurances and Far Eastern Commission discussions. Britain fears preparations advanced before interested governments were consulted.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Commission discussion of Japanese fishing areas
subfiles.about: A subcommittee seeks compromise on whether extensions of Japanese fishing areas need FEC approval.
subfiles.summary: The United States stresses Japan's need for fish and SCAP flexibility. Members discuss a possible distance limit from foreign land and request food and catch data.

subfiles.title: Urgent inquiry from SCAP on whaling
subfiles.about: SCAP asks whether its June 13 telegram arrived and requests instructions.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson presses for an early answer on Antarctic whaling.

subfiles.title: Australian proposal to operate Japanese whaling vessels
subfiles.about: Plimsoll informally proposes Australian operation of a Japanese whaling unit.
subfiles.summary: Australia would allocate products to Japan; Whitman raises questions about other vessels, meat and leasing.

subfiles.title: Australian mission proposal and SCAP response
subfiles.about: Transmits an Australian proposal to conduct the expedition and SCAP's rejection of it.
subfiles.summary: Australia offers to use Japanese vessels while supplying food products to Japan. SCAP replies that Australian control offers no advantage, conflicts with occupation authority, and would delay preparations too long for the coming season.

subfiles.title: Lykke presents Norwegian protest
subfiles.about: Lykke delivers Norway's protest and argues that fishing could supply Japan's protein.
subfiles.summary: Allison promises to circulate the Norwegian aide-mémoire and remarks.

subfiles.title: Norwegian protest against Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Norway asks the United States to withdraw consent for the 1947–48 Japanese expedition.
subfiles.summary: Norway cites security, conservation and poor oil recovery. It proposes intensified fisheries for protein and direct tanker delivery of Japan's allotted whale oil.

subfiles.title: United States explanation to Norway of whaling authorization
subfiles.about: Explains why the United States authorized a second SCAP-controlled expedition.
subfiles.summary: The United States cites Japan's need for protein and oil, the cost of relief imports, and opposition to excluding Japan from peaceful trade. It promises international regulation, equipment changes, inspectors and security controls, while reserving the long-term question for Allied decision.

subfiles.title: United States reply to Norwegian protest
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Norway's objections while maintaining authorization of the second expedition.
subfiles.summary: The United States says Norway's views received careful consideration before the decision.

subfiles.title: Australian protest and alternative whaling proposal
subfiles.about: Australia protests the decision and offers to operate Japanese whaling vessels.
subfiles.summary: Australia proposes using a factory ship and chasers, alone or with other Allies, while allocating food to Japan. It objects that authorization was announced while its alternative was under discussion and asks that vessel preparation not preclude transfer.

subfiles.title: Makin's conversation with the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Australian Ambassador Makin presents further objections to Japanese Antarctic whaling.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary says he will consider Makin's points seriously.

subfiles.title: Australian Ambassador's speaking notes on whaling
subfiles.about: Sets out Australia's security and political objections and supports an Australian-run expedition.
subfiles.summary: The notes contend that Australia could meet Japan's food needs without delay, yield more oil and avoid the perceived naval and espionage threat of Japanese vessels near Australia.

subfiles.title: Proposed reply to Australian aide-mémoire
subfiles.about: Recommends delivering a formal rejection of Australia's proposal after consulting MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur opposes the proposal; the attached reply is recommended for delivery to Makin.

subfiles.title: Briefing for meeting with Ambassador Makin
subfiles.about: Prepares the Secretary for Makin's further protest and a possible request for FEC decision.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews British and Australian moves, including a request to countermand MacArthur's instructions. It defends Japanese participation in peaceful industry and attaches a proposed reply.

subfiles.title: United States rejection of Australian whaling proposal
subfiles.about: Explains why the United States will retain the SCAP-controlled expedition.
subfiles.summary: The reply recounts consultations and the timing of Australia's proposal. It argues that the Japanese-run expedition supplies food and foreign exchange, poses no apparent security threat under SCAP control, and supports Japan's economic recovery.

subfiles.title: Alternative draft passage rejecting Australian proposal
subfiles.about: Drafts an additional argument against transferring Japanese whaling operations to Australia.
subfiles.summary: Warns that the proposal could seem to exploit Japan's defeated status for commercial advantage.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding whaling authorization records
subfiles.about: Forwards the Allied Council memorandum, SCAP directive and press release for the record.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson encloses records announcing the second expedition.

subfiles.title: Notice to Allied Council members
subfiles.to: Members of the Allied Council for Japan
subfiles.about: Notifies members of the directive authorizing the second expedition.
subfiles.summary: The authorization follows United States instructions after discussions with interested governments.

subfiles.title: SCAP directive authorizing 1947–48 Antarctic whaling
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Authorizes a Japanese expedition and specifies its area, reporting and security conditions.
subfiles.summary: The directive defines the Antarctic operating area, requires approval of vessels and routes, daily radio reports, international-rule compliance and controlled storage of whale oil. It says the authorization establishes no precedent for later seasons or territorial claims.

subfiles.title: Public announcement of second whaling expedition
subfiles.from: Far East Command Public Information Office
subfiles.about: Announces authorization and gives food, oil and financial reasons for the expedition.
subfiles.summary: The release predicts meat and oil output comparable to the previous season and promises Allied supervision.

subfiles.title: Record copy replacement notice
subfiles.about: Marks a white telegram copy as the record copy.
subfiles.summary: Replacement notice for an unreturned yellow action copy.

subfiles.title: Australian press reaction to whaling decision
subfiles.about: Reports Australian newspaper criticism and public statements by Evatt and Chifley.
subfiles.summary: Canberra and Sydney papers criticize the United States decision and its handling of consultation. Evatt promotes Australia's alternative and FEC review.

subfiles.title: British effort to postpone FEC whaling vote
subfiles.about: Reports Bevin's effort to avoid a Far Eastern Commission vote on the British whaling proposal.
subfiles.summary: Britain fears a United States veto would create an unwelcome precedent and seeks time for a negotiated compromise.

subfiles.title: New Zealand protest against second expedition
subfiles.about: New Zealand protests unilateral authorization and supports Australia's alternative.
subfiles.summary: The note cites security and conservation while denying any wish to profit economically from Japan's defeat.

subfiles.title: United States reply to New Zealand protest
subfiles.about: Defends the consultation process and rejection of the Australian alternative.
subfiles.summary: The reply traces exchanges from May through June and says interested governments had time to present objections and alternatives. It describes further review after the Australian offer, cites food, foreign-exchange and recovery benefits, and finds no sufficient security reason to cancel the expedition.

subfiles.title: Copy of New Zealand protest
subfiles.about: Duplicates New Zealand's protest and support for an Allied-operated expedition.
subfiles.summary: Copy of the June 25 New Zealand aide-mémoire.

subfiles.title: Evatt statement released in Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits an Australian statement criticizing unilateral authorization and urging FEC review.
subfiles.summary: Evatt reviews the 1946 expedition, consultation assurances, security concerns, alleged waste and Australia's offer to operate a whaling unit. He argues that future Japanese whaling and vessel disposal should be decided by the Allies.

subfiles.title: Japanese shore-whaling statistics for 1946
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards statistics supplied to the International Bureau for Whaling Statistics.
subfiles.summary: The report lists 19 shore stations, 41 killer boats, species catches and production of oil, meat and other whale products.

subfiles.title: Record copy replacement notice
subfiles.about: Marks a white telegram copy as the record copy.
subfiles.summary: Replacement notice for an unreturned yellow action copy.

subfiles.title: SCAP request to counter Allied criticism
subfiles.about: Asks the Department to counter British and Australian criticism of SCAP.
subfiles.summary: The request concerns Antarctic whaling and the Angaur phosphate project.

subfiles.title: The Economist on Japanese whaling controversy
subfiles.about: Quotes an article on conservation, consultation and Dominion strategic objections.
subfiles.summary: The article criticizes Japanese whaling methods and unilateral United States action, suggesting shore operations and wider Allied participation in decisions about Japan's merchant fleet.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Commission debate on Japanese whaling
subfiles.about: Summarizes the June 26 FEC debate and its decision to postpone further whaling discussion.
subfiles.summary: Australia, New Zealand and Britain criticize the expedition; other members express varied reservations. The FEC postpones the British proposal while diplomatic talks continue. The final page adds an unrelated decision on temporary retention of electric steel furnaces.
